summary: On a Sabbath, with His critics watching to accuse Him, Jesus restores a man’s withered hand in the synagogue, and the Pharisees begin plotting His death.
key_insight: Jesus asked whether it was lawful on the Sabbath “to save life or to kill.” That same Sabbath He restored a man, and the men who objected went out to plan how to destroy Him. His question answered itself before the day was over.
story: On another Sabbath Jesus went into the synagogue and taught. {Lk} A man was there whose right hand was withered. {Lk}

The scribes and Pharisees {Lk} watched Him closely to see whether He would heal on the Sabbath, so that they might accuse Him. They put their question to Him: “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?” {Mt} But Jesus knew their thoughts. He said to the man with the withered hand, “Arise and stand here,” and he got up and stood in front of them all. {Lk}

Then Jesus turned the question back on them: “Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do evil, to save life or to kill?” But they kept silent. {Mk} “What man is there among you who has one sheep, and if it falls into a pit on the Sabbath, will not lay hold of it and lift it out? Of how much more value then is a man than a sheep? Therefore it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath.” {Mt}
He looked around at them with anger, grieved by the hardness of their hearts. {Mk} Then He said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” He stretched it out, and it was restored as whole as the other.
The leaders were filled with rage {Lk} and went out. At once the Pharisees began to plot with the Herodians against Jesus, how they might destroy Him. {Mk}
differences: In Matthew the leaders ask Jesus, “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?” In Mark and Luke, Jesus asks them whether it is lawful to do good or evil on the Sabbath.
Only Matthew records the example of the sheep fallen into a pit.
Only Mark tells of Jesus’ anger and grief at the hardness of their hearts, and only Mark names the Herodians.

Luke alone says it was the man’s right hand and that Jesus knew their thoughts. Where Matthew and Mark say the Pharisees plotted to destroy Him, Luke says they were filled with rage and discussed what they might do to Jesus.

fit.question: Who asked the question about the Sabbath? In Matthew the Pharisees ask Jesus. In Mark and Luke, Jesus asks them.

points.label: Question and counter-question
points.text: The leaders opened with their test: “Is it lawful to heal on the Sabbath?” (Matthew 12:10). Jesus answered, as He often did, with a sharper question of His own (compare Mark 11:29–30). Matthew records their question; Mark and Luke record His.

points.label: One exchange, remembered in parts
points.text: Matthew keeps the sheep in the pit and the conclusion, “it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath.” Mark and Luke keep the question that silenced the room. All of it fits one short, tense exchange.

fit.note: The writers record different lines from one conversation, and the lines fit together naturally.
fit.short: The leaders asked their test question; Jesus answered with a question of His own. Matthew records theirs, Mark and Luke record His.

scene.label: Healing that could wait
scene.text: A withered hand was shrunken and useless, but it did not threaten the man’s life. The leaders’ tradition allowed treatment on the Sabbath only when life was in danger, so in their view this cure could have waited a day.

scene.label: A sheep in a pit
scene.text: Jesus’ question assumes that His hearers would rescue a sheep on the Sabbath without a second thought. The stricter community behind the Dead Sea Scrolls forbade even that, but the men in this synagogue would not have argued.

scene.label: The Herodians
scene.text: These were supporters of the Herod family, which ruled Galilee through Herod Antipas. Pharisees normally kept their distance from them. That the two groups now joined forces shows how far the opposition to Jesus had gone.

witnesses.matthew: Records the leaders’ test question and the argument from the sheep, ending with a plain rule: “it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath.” Right after the plot, Matthew quotes Isaiah’s gentle Servant who will not break a bruised reed (12:17–21; see event 43), a quiet contrast to men planning His death.
witnesses.mark: Lets the reader see Jesus’ face: He looked around at them with anger, grieved by the hardness of their hearts. Mark ends the story with religious and political rivals joined in the first plot against Jesus’ life (3:6), only three chapters into his Gospel.
witnesses.luke: Notes that it was the man’s right hand and that Jesus knew what His critics were thinking. Luke says they were “filled with rage” and only discussed what to do, then moves straight to Jesus praying all night before He chose the Twelve.

seeing.reveals: Jesus is angry at hard hearts and grieved by them at the same moment, and He heals the man in front of them all. He does good on the Sabbath knowing it will be used against Him.
seeing.living: The leaders saw the man as evidence for a charge; Jesus called him into the middle of the room and made him whole. Do not treat people as cases to win, and when a chance to do good is in front of you, do not hide behind a rule to avoid it.
seeing.ponder: Is there a place where your heart has grown hard, so that you would rather be right than see someone made whole?

preaching.big_idea: Jesus chose to do good on the Sabbath, while hardened hearts chose to destroy.
outline: A man in need and a room full of watchers (1–2)
A question that exposes the heart (3–4)
Anger, grief and a restoring word (5)
preaching.watch_for: Notice the eyes in the passage. The critics “watched Him closely” (v. 2), but Jesus “looked around at them” (v. 5) and saw the hardness of their hearts. The watchers are the ones being examined.
